text: Where do you live?
I live in Hangzhou, in the east of China. It's a big city, but my flat is near a quiet lake.
Do you work or are you a student?
I'm a student. I'm in my second year at secondary school, and my favourite subject is science.
Do you enjoy studying English?
Yes, I do, because I like watching films in English, and I can understand more of them now.
What did you do last weekend?
On Saturday I went cycling with my cousin, and on Sunday I stayed at home and helped my mum cook.
In the picture, I can see a teenage boy sitting at a desk in his bedroom.
He is writing something in a notebook, and there is an open laptop next to him.
He is wearing a green hoodie, and he has headphones around his neck.
On the wall behind him, there are some posters of football players.
There is a bookshelf on the left with lots of books and a few small trophies.
A guitar is standing in the corner next to the window, and the curtains are open.
It looks like the afternoon, because the sun is shining into the room.
The room is a bit untidy, with some clothes on the bed.
I think he is doing his homework, and he seems quite relaxed.
A new girl called Mia has just joined our class. How could we help her feel welcome?
Well, we could invite her to have lunch with us. That's an easy way to start talking.
Yes, that's simple and friendly. We could also show her around the school on her first day.
Good idea, because she probably doesn't know where the library or the sports hall is.
What about organising something at the weekend, like a trip to the cinema?
That might be too soon. She may feel shy going out with people she has just met.
Fair enough. Then we could tell her about the school clubs, so she meets people with the same interests.
I like that. And if she has missed some lessons, we could help her with the work.
True, but let's not do everything at once. Lunch and the tour are the most important on day one.
I agree, and then we can mention the clubs and the weekend later, when she feels more comfortable.
So we both think inviting her to lunch and showing her around are the best ways to start.
Exactly. Let's talk to her tomorrow morning before the first lesson.
Tell us about the place where you live.
I live in a flat on the tenth floor. It has three bedrooms, and my room looks out over a park.
Which is your favourite room at home, and why?
The kitchen, because that's where my family spends most of our time together, especially at dinner.
Is there anything you don't like about your home?
The lift is often broken, so sometimes I have to walk up ten floors, which is really tiring.
Would you prefer to live in a house or a flat in the future?
I'd prefer a house with a garden, because I'd love to have a dog and grow some vegetables.
In this picture, I can see three people in a living room at home.
A man is sitting on a grey sofa reading a newspaper, and he looks very comfortable.
On the carpet, a little girl is playing with a black cat and a piece of string.
Near the window, a woman is watering some plants.
There is a big bookshelf full of books, and a lamp next to the sofa.
There are some family photos on the wall, and the TV in the corner is switched off.
The girl is wearing pyjamas, so it is probably the morning or the evening.
Everything looks clean and tidy, and the colours in the room are warm.
I think it is a quiet moment at home, and everyone seems relaxed.
My parents want to do something with the empty room at home, and they've asked for ideas. What do you think?
Well, a study would be really useful. You'd have a quiet place to do your homework.
That's true, but I already do my homework at the kitchen table, and it works fine.
OK. Then what about a guest room? Your grandparents could stay when they visit.
They only visit twice a year, though, so the room would be empty most of the time.
Good point. A small gym could be nice, with a bike and some weights.
I'm not sure my family would use it. Nobody at home really likes exercise!
Ha! Then a games room might be more popular, with a big screen and some comfortable chairs.
I'd love that, but my parents will probably say it's a waste of space.
Maybe, but the last option, using it just for storage, sounds a bit boring.
I agree. Honestly, I still think the games room would make everyone happiest.
And I'd still choose the study. Let's give your parents both ideas and let them decide.
Do you do any sport?
Yes, I play badminton twice a week at a sports centre near my school, and I sometimes go running in the park.
Do you prefer playing sport or watching it?
Playing, definitely, because when I watch a match on TV I just want to get up and move.
Is there a sport you would like to try in the future?
I'd like to try climbing, because a new climbing centre has opened in my town and my friends say it's exciting.
Do you think young people do enough exercise these days?
Not really. Most of my classmates spend hours on their phones, so I think schools should offer more sport after lessons.
In this picture, there are some teenagers playing basketball on an outdoor court.
A girl in a red shirt is jumping up and throwing the ball towards the basket.
Two players in blue are trying to stop her.
It looks like a warm day, because everyone is wearing shorts and T-shirts.
Behind the court, there is a tall fence and a row of trees.
Some students are sitting on a bench at the side, watching the game and holding water bottles.
On the ground, I can see a few bags and a jacket that someone has taken off.
The court has white lines and a dark green floor, and the basket is on a metal pole.
Everyone looks very focused, so I think it's an important game for them.
The school wants students to do more exercise, and these are the ideas. Which one do you think would work best?
A running club before school sounds healthy, but I'm not sure many people would get up early for it.
I agree, most of us are tired enough in the morning. Dance or yoga classes after school might be more popular.
That's a nice idea, especially for people who don't like team sports.
What about a sports competition between classes every month?
That could be fun, but only the good players would take part, and the others would just watch.
True. Weekend hikes would get everyone walking, and you don't need to be good at anything.
I like hiking, though not everyone can come at the weekend because of family plans.
The last idea is opening the sports hall at lunchtime, so people can play whenever they want.
That's the simplest one, and it doesn't cost the school anything.
So maybe the best plan is opening the hall at lunchtime, plus a dance or yoga class after school.
Yes, I think those two together would get the most students moving.
How do you usually travel to school?
I take the underground, and then I walk for about ten minutes. It's crowded, but it's much faster than the bus.
Which do you prefer, travelling by train or by car?
I prefer the train, because I can read or sleep, and I don't have to worry about traffic.
Is it easy to get around your town?
Yes, mostly. There are lots of buses and shared bikes, but the traffic is terrible in the evening.
Have you ever been on a long journey?
Yes, last summer I took a high-speed train to Beijing with my family, and I loved watching the countryside go past.
In the picture, I can see a bus stop on a busy street in a city.
Four or five people are waiting under a small shelter, and a red bus is just arriving.
It is raining, so most of them are holding umbrellas or wearing raincoats.
A young man at the front is looking at his phone.
Next to him, an older woman is carrying two shopping bags and a black umbrella.
Behind the shelter, there are some tall buildings and a shop with bright lights.
The road is wet, and I can see the lights of some cars in the distance.
There is a rubbish bin and a timetable on a pole next to the shelter.
I think it is the evening after work, and everyone wants to get home quickly.
We're all going to Suzhou for the day on Saturday. How should we travel there?
The train is the obvious choice. It only takes about an hour, and it's never late.
It's quite expensive for six people, though. The coach is much cheaper.
That's true, but the coach can get stuck in traffic, and someone always feels sick on it.
What if we ask my dad to drive us? Then we could stop wherever we want.
Six of us won't fit in one car, and I don't think he'd want to spend his Saturday driving.
Fair point. Cycling would be an adventure, but it's about eighty kilometres.
Eighty kilometres! We'd arrive too tired to do anything.
OK, so it's really between the train and the coach.
If we book early, the train tickets are cheaper, and we'd have more time in the city.
That's a good point. More time there matters more than saving a little money.
So let's go by train, and I'll check the ticket prices tonight.
Which festival do you enjoy most, and why?
Spring Festival, definitely. My relatives all come to my grandma's house, and we cook and eat together for days.
How do you usually celebrate your birthday?
I usually invite a few close friends round, and we order pizza and watch a film together.
Did you do anything special last Spring Festival?
Yes, we visited my aunt in the countryside, and we set off fireworks by the river, which was amazing.
Do you think festivals are important for families?
Yes, I think so, because everyone is so busy during the year, and festivals give us time to relax and talk.
In the picture, I can see a birthday party in a garden on a sunny day.
A girl of about ten is blowing out the candles on a big chocolate cake.
Around her, there are six or seven children wearing party hats, and they are all clapping.
On the table, there are some cups, crisps and sandwiches.
There are colourful balloons tied to the chairs, and a banner that says Happy Birthday.
A woman on the left is taking a photo with her phone, and she is smiling.
In the background, there is a wooden fence and a tree with a swing.
The girl is wearing a yellow dress, and she looks very excited.
I think it is a lovely afternoon, and everyone is having a great time.
The school is planning a Mid-Autumn Festival evening for the exchange students. Which activities should we include?
Making mooncakes together would be great. Everyone loves food, and it's easy to join in.
True, but the kitchen is small, and thirty people can't cook at the same time.
OK, then what about a lantern workshop? People could make their own and carry them outside later.
I like that. It's creative, and the lanterns would look beautiful in the dark.
We could also ask the music club to play some traditional songs.
That sounds nice, though a whole concert might be a bit long for people who don't know the music.
Maybe just two or three songs, then. And someone could tell the story behind the festival.
Yes, a short story would help the exchange students understand why we celebrate it.
The last idea is a picnic outside to look at the moon. That's what the festival is really about.
I'd put the picnic first, because it's the most relaxed way for everyone to talk.
And I'd choose the lanterns, because people take something home. Let's suggest both and let the teachers decide.
Tell us about a good friend of yours.
My best friend is Kevin. We met in primary school, and we've been friends for nearly eight years.
What do you usually do together?
We play basketball after school, and at the weekend we often go to the cinema or just chat at his place.
Is it easy to make new friends?
Not really, because I'm quite quiet when I meet new people, but once I know someone I talk a lot.
Do you think it's important to have a lot of friends?
Not really. I think two or three close friends you can trust are better than a hundred people you hardly know.
In this picture, two girls are sitting at a small table in a café.
One of them is showing something on her phone, and the other is laughing.
They both have a coffee, and there is a piece of cake in the middle of the table.
The girl on the right has curly hair and is wearing a white jumper.
Behind them, there is a big window, and I can see people walking past in the street.
The café looks small and cosy, with wooden tables and some plants on the shelves.
On the wall, there is a blackboard with the menu written on it.
It looks like a cloudy afternoon, because the light outside is quite soft.
I think they are close friends, and they are enjoying their time together.
Lucy is moving to Shanghai next month. How can we make sure we stay in touch with her?
A video call every week would be the best way. You can see her face and really talk.
I agree, though we'd have to find a time that works for everyone, because she'll have a new school.
That's true. A group chat is easier, because people can send messages whenever they're free.
Yes, but group chats go quiet after a few weeks. Everyone just sends stickers.
Ha, that's exactly what happens! Visiting her in the holidays would be more special.
Definitely, and Shanghai is only an hour away by train, so it's not difficult.
What about writing letters or sending postcards? It's old-fashioned, but it's fun to get real post.
I like that, but honestly I'd forget to write after the first one.
Fair enough. Watching a film online together at the same time could be fun too.
So a weekly video call plus visits in the holidays seems like the best plan.
I agree, and we can keep the group chat for everyday things in between.
